overview.en: J. J. Thomson was an English physicist who discovered the electron in 1897, fundamentally changing our understanding of atomic structure. He won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1906 and led the Cavendish Laboratory during one of its most productive periods.

early_life.en: Born in Cheetham Hill, Manchester, Thomson entered Owens College at age 14 and later studied at Trinity College, Cambridge. He became Cavendish Professor of Physics at Cambridge at the remarkably young age of 28.

impact.en: Thomson's discovery of the electron proved that atoms are not indivisible and opened the era of subatomic physics. His plum pudding model of the atom, while later superseded, was the first attempt to describe internal atomic structure and inspired Rutherford's nuclear model.

event.en: Became Cavendish Professor of Physics at Cambridge at age 28.
Discovered the electron through cathode ray experiments.
Proposed the plum pudding model of the atom.
Awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on electrical conductivity in gases.
Discovered the existence of isotopes through positive ray analysis.

description.en: Landmark paper announcing the discovery of the electron and measuring its charge-to-mass ratio.

title.en: On the Structure of the Atom

description.en: Paper proposing the plum pudding model of atomic structure.

title.en: Rays of Positive Electricity and Their Application to Chemical Analyses

description.en: Work describing the discovery of isotopes using positive ray analysis.

text.en: Could anything at first sight seem more impractical than a body which is so small that its mass is an insignificant fraction of the mass of an atom of hydrogen?
